title: Revoking a certificate
summary: When a key leaks, the certificate must stop being trusted before its end date: revoke it, publish a CRL, and check against it.

scheme: → revoke it: the CA lists it as revoked
text: A certificate stays valid until its end date, even when its key leaked. Revoking it is the CA saying: don't trust this one any more.
- Revoke when a key leaks, or when a certificate was made by mistake.
- Then make a new key and a new certificate: revoking replaces nothing.
openssl ca -revoke marks the certificate R in index.txt. Clients never see that file: -gencrl publishes the list, a CRL, signed by the CA.
- A CRL has a next update date: publish the next one before it, or the clients that check it refuse every certificate.
A CRL lists serial numbers. openssl crl reads it; openssl verify checks a certificate against it.
- Make it again before its Next Update (default_crl_days in ca.cnf): a timer does it, like renewals.
- error 23: certificate revoked. Without a CRL, -crl_check fails too: unable to get certificate CRL.
- Where to fetch the CRL is usually written in the certificate: -ext crlDistributionPoints (Mac: read it in -text). Your CA adds it with crlDistributionPoints = URI:http://… in its section.

scheme: CRL    a list the CA publishes; clients
OCSP   asks the CA about one certificate,
live: the CA sees which site
text: OCSP asked the CA about a certificate at each visit: slow, and the CA learned which sites you visit. Public CAs now publish CRLs, and browsers keep their own lists, updated in the background (Firefox: CRLite).
- Short lifetimes are the other answer: public certificates last 200 days at most now, 47 from 2029-03-15, and a short one rarely needs revoking.
- For your private CA: publish the CRL where the clients that check it can fetch it.
